rewritten_text:
‘Stop the right paddle! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the left paddle! Right paddle forward! Stop her! Let the outside paddle turn slowly! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get that front rope out! Hurry up! Come on, bring out the side rope—what are you doing? Loop it around that stump! Ready with the gangplank—lower it! Engines finished, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!’ He was imitating the steam escaping from the test valves.

Tom continued whitewashing the fence without taking any notice of the steamboat. Ben stared for a moment. ‘Ha! You’re stuck, aren’t you!’ he said.

Tom did not answer. He studied his latest brushstroke like an artist, added another gentle stroke, and studied that too. Ben came alongside him. Tom longed for the apple, but kept working. Ben said:

‘Hello, old fellow. Got to work, have you?’

Tom turned around suddenly.

‘Oh, it’s you, Ben! I didn’t see you.’

‘Listen, I’m going swimming. Don’t you wish you could come? But naturally you’d rather work, wouldn’t you? Of course you would!’

Tom looked at him for a moment before answering.

‘What do you call work?’

‘Well, isn’t that work?’

Tom began painting again and replied casually:

‘Maybe it is and maybe it isn’t. All I know is, Tom Sawyer is happy with it.’

‘Oh, come on. You’re not trying to tell me you like it?’

The brush kept moving.

‘Like it? I don’t see why I shouldn’t. Does a boy get to whitewash a fence every day?’

That made the job look different. Ben stopped eating his apple. Tom moved the brush carefully back and forth, stepped away to examine his work, added a little here and there, and checked it again. Ben watched every movement, growing more interested and absorbed. Eventually he spoke.

‘Say, Tom, let me paint a bit.’

Tom thought about it and seemed ready to agree, but then changed his mind.

‘No, no, Ben, I don’t think I can. Aunt Polly is terribly fussy about this fence, right here beside the street. If it were the back fence, I wouldn’t mind, and neither would she. But she’s very particular about this one. It has to be done carefully. I don’t think one boy in a thousand, maybe even two thousand, could do it properly.’

‘Really? Is that true? Oh, come on, just let me try a little. I’d let you if I were in your place, Tom.’

‘Ben, I honestly would like to. But Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let him. Sid wanted a turn, and she wouldn’t let him either.’

‘Shall I visit them? Or Miss Bates? She lives even nearer. And I think she is as likely as anyone to know what the other people would prefer. We really need more opinions. Suppose I go and ask Miss Bates to join us?’

‘Well, if you like,’ Mrs. Weston said with some hesitation, ‘if you think she can help.’

‘You will get no useful answer from Miss Bates,’ Emma said. ‘She will be delighted and grateful, but she will tell you nothing. She will not even listen to your questions. I cannot see any point in asking her advice.’

‘But she is so entertaining, so wonderfully entertaining! I love hearing Miss Bates talk. Besides, I don’t have to bring the entire family.’

Mr. Weston joined them at this point. When he heard the proposal, he approved it strongly.

‘Yes, do, Frank. Fetch Miss Bates, and let us settle everything at once. I am sure she will enjoy the plan, and I cannot think of anyone better able to show us how to overcome our difficulties. Fetch her. We are becoming rather too particular. She is a constant example of how to be happy. But bring them both. Invite both of them.’

‘Both, sir? Can the old lady—?’

‘The old lady! No, the young lady, of course. I shall think you a great fool, Frank, if you bring the aunt without her niece.’

‘Oh, forgive me, sir. I didn’t think of her at once. Certainly, if that is what you wish, I will try to persuade them both.’ He hurried away.

Long before he returned with the short, tidy, briskly moving aunt and her elegant niece, Mrs. Weston had examined the passage again. Being a good-natured woman and a good wife, she now found its problems much smaller than she had first imagined—very minor indeed. That settled the difficult decisions. Everything else appeared, at least in theory, perfectly straightforward. The smaller arrangements—tables and chairs, lighting and music, tea and supper—seemed to arrange themselves, or were left as little matters that Mrs. Weston and Mrs. Stokes could settle at any time. Everyone invited would certainly attend. Frank had already written to Enscombe, asking to extend his fortnight’s visit by a few days, a request that could not possibly be refused. The dance would be delightful.

When Miss Bates arrived, she agreed with all her heart. They no longer needed her advice, but her approval, a far safer contribution, was very welcome. She praised both the whole plan and every detail, warmly and without stopping, and they could not help being pleased. For another half hour they all walked back and forth among the rooms. Some offered suggestions, others listened, and everyone happily imagined the pleasures to come.

A beard and mustache concealed more than half his deeply sunburned face. He carried a heavy oak club but seemed otherwise unarmed. Bowing awkwardly, he wished us good evening in French. His accent had something of Neuchâtel about it, yet still clearly suggested that he came from Paris.

‘Please sit down, my friend,’ Dupin said. ‘I assume you have come about the orangutan. I must say, I almost envy you owning him: a remarkably fine animal, and undoubtedly a valuable one. How old would you say he is?’

The sailor breathed deeply, like a man suddenly freed from an unbearable weight, then answered with renewed confidence.

‘I have no way of knowing, but he can’t be more than four or five years old. Is he here?’

‘Oh, no. We had no suitable place to keep him here. He is at a livery stable nearby, in the Rue Dubourg. You can collect him tomorrow morning. Naturally, you are prepared to prove that he belongs to you?’

‘Certainly I am, sir.’

‘I shall be sorry to let him go,’ said Dupin.

‘I don’t expect you to have taken all this trouble for nothing, sir,’ the man said. ‘That wouldn’t be reasonable. I’m quite willing to offer a reward for finding him—anything within reason, that is.’

‘Well,’ my friend replied, ‘that is certainly fair. Let me think. What should I ask for? Ah, I know. This will be my reward: tell me everything you know about the murders in the Rue Morgue.’

Dupin spoke those last words softly and with complete calm. Just as calmly, he went to the door, locked it, and slipped the key into his pocket. He then drew a pistol from inside his coat and laid it on the table without the slightest agitation.

The sailor’s face reddened as though he were choking. He sprang up and seized his club, but a moment later sank back into his chair, shaking violently, his face as pale as death. He said nothing. I pitied him with all my heart.

‘My friend,’ Dupin said gently, ‘you are frightening yourself needlessly. You really are. We have no intention of harming you. I give you my word, as a gentleman and a Frenchman, that we mean you no injury. I know perfectly well that you are innocent of the atrocities in the Rue Morgue. You cannot, however, deny that you are involved in them to some degree.’
